prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, but must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
# ARGUMENT

## I. A Plaintiff Need Not Plead a Prima Facie Case to Survive Rule 12(b)(6); She Must Allege Facts That Plausibly Support an Inference of Discrimination.

### A. The prima facie case is an evidentiary framework, not a pleading requirement.

This Court reviews de novo a dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), accepting well-pleaded facts as true and drawing all reasonable inferences for the plaintiff. *Robinson v. Am. Honda Motor Co.*, 551 F.3d 218, 222 (4th Cir. 2009); *Nemet Chevrolet, Ltd. v. Consumeraffairs.com, Inc.*, 591 F.3d 250, 255 (4th Cir. 2009). A complaint survives if it contains sufficient factual matter to state a claim that is plausible on its face. *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009); *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007).

The Supreme Court has held that the *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie case "is an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). *Twombly* reaffirmed that holding. 550 U.S. at 569–70. This Court has applied it consistently. In *Coleman v. Maryland Court of Appeals*, the Court explained that a Title VII plaintiff is not required to plead facts constituting a prima facie case to survive a motion to dismiss. 626 F.3d 187, 190 (4th Cir. 2010), *aff'd*, 566 U.S. 30 (2012). *McCleary-Evans v. Maryland Department of Transportation, State Highway Administration* repeated the rule. 780 F.3d 582, 584 (4th Cir. 2015). So did *Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 648 (4th Cir. 2017), and *Bing v. Brivo Systems, LLC*, 959 F.3d 605, 616–17 (4th Cir. 2020).

The reason is practical. The prima facie framework allocates burdens of production after discovery. It does not measure the sufficiency of a complaint. Requiring a plaintiff to plead each prima facie element, before discovery of the employer's decision-making and comparator information, would impose a heightened pleading standard that Rule 8(a)(2) does not permit. *Swierkiewicz*, 534 U.S. at 512–13.

### B. The complaint must still allege facts that make discrimination plausible.

Eliminating the prima facie pleading requirement does not relieve a plaintiff of Rule 8. A complaint must "allege facts to satisfy the elements of a cause of action created by [the] statute." *McCleary-Evans*, 780 F.3d at 585; *accord Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190–91; *Bing*, 959 F.3d at 617. In a discrimination case, that means pleading facts that permit a reasonable inference that the adverse action occurred *because of* a protected characteristic. Legal conclusions and bare recitals of the elements do not suffice. *Iqbal*, 556 U.S. at 678–79; *Francis v. Giacomelli*, 588 F.3d 186, 193 (4th Cir. 2009). This Court has also stressed that plausibility is assessed on the complaint as a whole, not by dissecting individual allegations. *See Goode v. Cent. Va. Legal Aid Soc'y, Inc.*, 807 F.3d 619, 626 (4th Cir. 2015).

*McCleary-Evans* illustrates the line. There, the plaintiff alleged only that she was qualified, that she was not selected, and that the decisionmakers must have been biased. The Court affirmed dismissal because the complaint offered no facts connecting the hiring decision to race or sex, and it was equally consistent with lawful explanations. 780 F.3d at 585–86. The deficiency was a lack of factual content supporting causation, not a missing prima facie element.

### C. Appellant's complaint satisfies this standard.

The district court erred by faulting Appellant for not pleading facts establishing each element of a prima facie case, such as [identify element, e.g., a similarly situated comparator]. [JA __.] That approach is the one *Swierkiewicz*, *Coleman*, and *Woods* reject. The proper question is whether the facts alleged, taken as true, make it plausible that Appellant was subjected to adverse treatment because of [protected characteristic].

The complaint answers that question. It alleges [summarize specific facts: protected status; qualifications and satisfactory performance; the adverse action; the timing; remarks or conduct by decisionmakers; more favorable treatment of employees outside the protected class; departures from policy]. [JA __.] Unlike the conclusory allegations in *McCleary-Evans*, these facts supply the link between the challenged action and the protected characteristic. At the pleading stage, Appellant is entitled to the reasonable inferences from them, and the district court was not permitted to weigh them against competing explanations the employer may later offer. *Nemet*, 591 F.3d at 255; *see Twombly*, 550 U.S. at 556 (plausibility "does not impose a probability requirement at the pleading stage").

The judgment of dismissal should be reversed.
